intro.html: Groups can welcome people or shut them out, and they can look outward at the wide world or turn inward. This topic gives you verbs for pushing people away and adjectives for narrow and wide horizons.

Keeping away or rejecting: shun (avoid), spurn (reject with scorn), snub (ignore coldly). Pushing out or down: ostracize (exclude from a group), banish (send away), alienate (drive away, make unfriendly), relegate (move to a lower place). Horizons: insular and parochial (narrow) versus cosmopolitan (worldly).

Some come with history. Insular comes from the Latin for island; ostracize from the pieces of broken pottery on which the citizens of ancient Athens wrote the name of someone to be sent away; cosmopolitan means “citizen of the world.”

words.def: to avoid on purpose, again and again
words.ex: After the food fight, the twins {shunned} the cafeteria for a week.
words.ctx: Though the old house was perfectly safe, the children {shunned} it, crossing the street rather than walk past its creaky gate.

mn.cue: SHOO and RUN: keep far away
mn.text: Every cat in the neighborhood takes the long way around grumpy Rufus’s yard: they {shun} it.

scene.alt: Two cats steer well clear of a yard where a grumpy dog sits behind the fence.

words.ex: She {spurned} his offer of help and fixed the flat tire herself.
words.ctx: The proud inventor {spurned} every offer to buy his idea, insisting that no amount of money could tempt him to give it up.

mn.text: Ivy offers Aunt Tia a homemade cookie, but Tia sniffs, turns up her nose and turns away: “Too plain for me.” She {spurns} it.

scene.alt: A girl offers a woman a cookie, and the woman turns away with her nose in the air.

words.def: to ignore or treat coldly on purpose
words.ex: Lila felt hurt when her old friend {snubbed} her at the party.
words.ctx: The new student greeted everyone warmly, so he was puzzled when the team captain {snubbed} him, turning away without a word.

mn.cue: a SNUB nose stuck in the air
mn.text: Jonah waves and calls, “Hi, Maya!” but she sticks her nose in the air and walks right past him: she {snubs} him.

scene.alt: A teen boy waves hello, but a girl walks past him with her nose in the air.

words.def: to shut someone out of a group
words.ex: No one should be {ostracized} for liking different music.
words.ctx: After he told the coach about the cheating, the other players {ostracized} him; no one sat with him at lunch or answered his messages for weeks.
words.etym: From Greek ostrakizein, from ostrakon (a piece of broken pottery): the citizens of ancient Athens voted to send someone away by writing the name on such pieces.

mn.cue: OSTRA-CIZE: shut OUT of the huddle
mn.text: The penguins huddle close together and turn their backs on little Pebble, who stands alone in the snow: they {ostracize} him.

scene.alt: Three penguins huddle with their backs turned while a small penguin stands alone and sad.

words.def: to send someone away as a punishment
words.ex: In the legend, the king {banished} the traitor to a faraway island.
words.ctx: The cat was {banished} from the kitchen after she knocked the cake off the counter, and she now sulks in the hallway at every mealtime.
words.etym: From Old French banir, “to proclaim, to outlaw,” related to ban.

mn.text: “You are banned from my kingdom!” the king declares, pointing at the gate, and the scheming Rex trudges off with his bag: the king {banishes} him.

scene.alt: A king points sternly toward the road as a man carrying a bag trudges away from the castle.

words.def: to make someone feel unwelcome, or to turn them against you
words.ctx: By changing the rules without asking anyone, the club president {alienated} her members; within a month, half of them had quit.
words.etym: From Latin alienare, “to make another’s, to estrange,” from alienus (of another).

mn.text: Dev brags and interrupts so much that his friends drift away one by one, until they feel like strangers: he {alienates} them.

scene.alt: A teen brags through a megaphone while his friends walk away from him.

words.def: to move to a lower place, rank or position
words.ex: The broken lamp was {relegated} to the attic.
words.ctx: After losing every game, the team was {relegated} to the lower league, where it would have to play weaker teams for a whole season.
words.etym: From Latin relegare, “to send away”: re- (away) + legare (to send).

mn.text: When Pip gets a shiny new robot, his old teddy is moved to the dusty top shelf at the back: the teddy is {relegated}.

scene.alt: A boy cheers over a new robot while his old teddy bear sits forgotten on a high shelf.

words.def: narrow in outlook; cut off from outside ideas
words.ex: The {insular} little town rarely welcomed visitors.
words.ctx: The club had grown {insular}; its members talked only to one another, ignored new ideas and hardly noticed when the rest of the school stopped coming.

mn.cue: INSUL = ISLAND: cut off from the world
mn.text: Grandpa Gus lives on his own little island and waves away every boat bringing news and new ideas: “No thanks!” His outlook is {insular}.

scene.alt: A grumpy man on a tiny island waves away a boat carrying a banner that says NEW IDEAS.

words.ex: My cousin’s {parochial} view was that nothing interesting ever happened outside our county.
words.ctx: The newspaper’s coverage was {parochial}, filling page after page with local bake sales while ignoring important events in the rest of the world.
words.etym: From Latin parochia, “parish,” a small local district.

mn.cue: can’t see past the village OAK: par-OAK-ial
mn.text: To Uncle Felix, the whole world stops at the old oak at the edge of the village; nothing beyond it interests him: his outlook is {parochial}.

scene.alt: A man points at the old oak at the edge of his village, sure there is nothing worth seeing beyond it.

words.def: familiar with many countries and cultures; worldly
words.ex: The {cosmopolitan} city had restaurants from forty countries on a single street.
words.ctx: Having lived in six countries and learned four languages, Aunt Lin was truly {cosmopolitan}, at ease in any crowd anywhere in the world.

roots.means: one who, having to do with

words.etym: From Greek kosmopolites, “citizen of the world”: kosmos (world) + polites (citizen).

mn.cue: COSMO = WORLD: a citizen of the world
mn.text: Aunt Lin’s suitcase is covered with stickers from a dozen countries, and she greets everyone in their own language: she is {cosmopolitan}.

scene.alt: A smiling traveler with a sticker-covered suitcase and a globe greets people in several languages.

after.cap: Ways of pushing people (and things) away.

after.html: Insular and parochial both mean narrow in outlook; cosmopolitan is their opposite. Parochial can also simply mean “of a parish,” as in a parochial school, with no criticism at all, so read the context.

opts.s: Traveling to twelve countries made Rosa far more {cosmopolitan} than her stay-at-home cousins.

items.q: In “She attended a parochial school,” parochial means…
items.why: Parochial first means “of a parish.” In other sentences it means narrow in outlook, so the context decides.
Insular comes from the Latin insula, island: an insular group is cut off like an island.

items.q: True or false: cosmopolitan is an opposite of parochial.
items.why: True. Cosmopolitan means worldly, at home in many cultures; parochial means narrow and local.

items.q: The star player was moved from the starting team to the bench. She was…
items.why: Being moved to a lower position is being relegated. She was not sent away or shut out of the team.
